procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 4, 1963, of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Revision No. 396 of 1962.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Magistrate convicted the respondent (Motilal Kanoria). The High Court of Calcutta acquitted the respondent and dismissed the revision.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (unspecified, but likely the prosecution) appealed to the Supreme Court by certificate under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution, challenging the Calcutta High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: whether by disposing of the imported goods without permission any offence was committed

facts: A company was granted an import license in May 1955, which stipulated that the imported goods were for the company's own use.
In December 1955, the Imports (Control) Order, 1955, came into force.
The license was revalidated in 1956, and after the goods arrived, the respondent sold them to another party, violating the 'own use' condition.
law: Section 5 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, makes it an offense to contravene any Order made under the Act.
The Imports (Control) Order, 1955, contained specific provisions:
Clause 12 (proviso): Made the 1955 Order applicable to licenses issued under previous orders.
Clause 5(3): Deemed certain conditions to be a part of every license.
Clause 5(4): Required every licensee to observe the conditions of their license.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had overlooked the proviso to clause 12 of the 1955 Order. This proviso meant that the 1955 Order applied to the license in question, even though it was granted before the Order was enacted.
The Court reasoned that because the 1955 Order applied, its clauses 5(3) and 5(4) effectively became part of the license conditions.
Consequently, when the respondent sold the goods, they were not merely breaching a condition of the license, but were also directly contravening clauses 5(3) and 5(4) of the 1955 Order itself.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the breach of the license condition amounted to a breach of the Imports (Control) Order, 1955. Since contravening an Order is an offense under Section 5 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, an offense was committed by disposing of the imported goods.

issue.issue_text: whether the respondent was personally liable

facts: The respondent (Kanoria) was a director of a company and a partner in its managing firm.
He personally handled the application for an import licence and the subsequent transfer (sale) of the imported goods, which was a violation of the licence's conditions.
He wrote every document connected with the issuance of the licence and the transfer of the goods.
Although the complaint against him was not perfectly clear, it described him as an accused, and he participated in the trial without objecting to this status.
law: Section 5 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act 1947 states that "if any person contravenes any order made or deemed to have been made... he shall be punishable".

Section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states that an error, omission, or irregularity in a complaint is curable and should not lead to a reversal of a finding unless it has caused a failure of justice.
application: The Court determined that the respondent was the person who actually performed the acts that led to the violation.

His actions were not considered mere abetment (assisting someone else) but were the direct cause of the contravention. The Court noted that the company could not have committed the offence if the respondent had not acted as he did.
Because he was directly responsible for the actions, the Court found him to be a "principal offender" along with the company.

Regarding the lack of clarity in the complaint, the Court found that since the respondent was described as an accused and did not object at trial, any error was curable under s. 537 and had not led to a failure of justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the respondent was personally liable as a principal offender because he was directly responsible for the actions that constituted the illegal transfer of goods, and any procedural defect in the complaint was a curable error that did not prejudice him.

arguments.issue_text: whether by disposing of the imported goods without permission any offence was committed
appellant_arguments: The disposal of imported goods without permission was a contravention of the conditions of the licence, which constituted an offence under Section 5 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act 1947, read with Clause 5 of the Imports (Control) Order 1955.
respondent_arguments: At the time the transaction of sale was entered into (December 1956), a breach of a condition of a licence did not constitute an offence under Section 5 of the Act of 1947.

arguments.issue_text: whether the respondent was personally liable
appellant_arguments: The respondent was responsible for the issuance of the licence and for the transfer of the goods imported under it, making him principally responsible along with the company.

Any error, omission, or irregularity in the complaint was curable under Section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the respondent was described as an accused, did not object at his trial, and there was no failure of justice.
respondent_arguments: The complaint was not clear as to whom was really meant to be prosecuted.

cases.principle: The case was applied in the context of determining whether the contravention of a condition of an import licence constitutes a punishable offense under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A license issued under a prior statutory order is deemed to have been issued under a subsequent, superseding order if the new order contains a proviso stating that actions taken under the prior order are considered taken under the corresponding provisions of the new one. Consequently, the conditions and prohibitions of the new order are incorporated into the pre-existing license, and a violation of those conditions constitutes an offense under the new order.
obiter: A condition in a license that affects the rights of parties is distinct from a condition imposed from a purely administrative point of view.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that an offence was committed because the licence, although granted before the Imports (Control) Order of 1955, was brought under its terms by the proviso to clause 12 of that Order. The 1955 Order, through clauses 5(3) and 5(4), incorporated the licence's conditions as part of the Order itself. Therefore, a breach of the licence condition (selling the goods) was a breach of the Order, which constituted a punishable offence under the governing Act.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation: The court analyzed whether a licence issued under a prior order came under the terms of the subsequent 1955 Order by interpreting the effect of its proviso clause.

Curable Defect (s. 537 Code of Criminal Procedure): The court assessed whether an error, omission, or irregularity in a complaint was fatal to the prosecution by determining if it had caused a failure of justice, particularly when the accused did not object during the trial.
policy_considerations: An error, omission, or irregularity in a complaint should not invalidate a conviction if it has not led to a failure of justice, especially when the accused was aware of being prosecuted and did not object at trial.
